title: Luke 22:54–71
context: Peter’s three denials fulfill Jesus’ warning and lead to bitter tears, while Jesus endures abuse and faces the council. His promise of exaltation stands against the verdict of his opponents. Both traditions take Peter’s sin and repentance seriously and locate restoration in grace rather than self-confidence. The narrative distinguishes hearing Christ from believing him and gives no warrant for blaming Jewish people collectively for the actions of the named authorities.

verses.text: They seized him and led him away, and brought him into the high priest’s house. But Peter followed from a distance.
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus is taken to the high priest’s house while Peter follows at a distance. Arminian readers see conflicted loyalty entering danger, not a detail that by itself establishes final apostasy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise recognize the beginning of Peter’s foretold failure. His distance neither excuses the denial nor cancels Christ’s prior promise of intercession and return.

verses.text: When they had kindled a fire in the middle of the courtyard and had sat down together, Peter sat among them.
verses.arminianNotes: Peter joins the people around the courtyard fire. Arminian readers attend to the ordinary social setting in which fear will test his promised loyalty.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see temptation unfolding through commonplace pressure rather than only spectacular attack. The narrative invites humility about how easily self-confidence can be exposed.

verses.text: A certain servant girl saw him as he sat in the light, and looking intently at him, said, “This man also was with him.”
verses.arminianNotes: A servant girl recognizes Peter’s association with Jesus. Arminian readers see a seemingly modest challenge revealing the need for courage supplied by grace.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note that Peter’s bold profession meets an ordinary witness rather than a mighty tribunal. His weakness exposes the limits of unaided resolve.

verses.text: He denied Jesus, saying, “Woman, I don’t know him.”
verses.arminianNotes: Peter explicitly denies knowing Jesus. Arminian readers take the sin seriously while reading it within the promised possibility of return through Christ’s gracious help.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise refuse to minimize denial. They distinguish this grievous fall from final loss of faith in light of Christ’s intercession and the restoration he announced.

verses.text: After a little while someone else saw him and said, “You also are one of them!” But Peter answered, “Man, I am not!”
verses.arminianNotes: A second identification draws another denial. Arminian readers see how fear can deepen sinful choices, strengthening the call to prayer rather than confidence in a past profession.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise recognize repeated failure in a disciple Christ will restore. Preservation does not mean that genuine believers cannot commit grave and repeated sins.

verses.text: After about one hour passed, another confidently affirmed, saying, “Truly this man also was with him, for he is a Galilean!”
verses.arminianNotes: Another witness confidently identifies Peter as a Galilean companion of Jesus. Arminian readers see continuing pressure exposing the difference between intended courage and tested fidelity.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise recognize the mounting evidence around Peter. The narrative unmasks self-reliance without portraying social pressure as an excuse that erases responsibility.

verses.text: But Peter said, “Man, I don’t know what you are talking about!” Immediately, while he was still speaking, a rooster crowed.
verses.arminianNotes: Peter’s third denial is immediately followed by the rooster’s crow. Arminian readers see Jesus’ warning confirmed, leaving no room to excuse the failure as insignificant.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise emphasize Christ’s truthful foreknowledge amid Peter’s collapse. The fulfilled prediction does not make the denial blameless; it prepares for the remembered word and repentance.

verses.text: The Lord turned and looked at Peter. Then Peter remembered the Lord’s word, how he said to him, “Before the rooster crows you will deny me three times.”
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus’ look recalls his warning to Peter’s mind. Arminian readers see gracious confrontation awakening recognition of sin, without speculating beyond what the narrative says about the look.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Christ’s remembered word interrupting denial. His preserving care does not leave Peter unchanged but brings his failure into the light.

verses.text: He went out, and wept bitterly.
verses.arminianNotes: Peter’s bitter tears mark grief over the denial. Arminian readers recognize repentance as a meaningful turn toward restoration, not a payment that makes forgiveness deserved.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise view his sorrow in light of Christ’s promised intercession. Grace brings the fallen disciple toward return without making tears themselves the ground of acceptance.

verses.text: The men who held Jesus mocked him and beat him.
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus is mocked and beaten by those holding him. Arminian readers see the innocent Savior enduring cruelty, not an event that makes his abusers morally innocent.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise affirm that redemptive purpose does not sanctify the perpetrators’ violence. Christ’s suffering exposes sin even as he continues the mission through which sinners are saved.

verses.text: Having blindfolded him, they struck him on the face and asked him, “Prophesy! Who is the one who struck you?”
verses.arminianNotes: The captors mock Jesus’ prophetic identity while concealing their blows. Arminian readers see abusive contempt, not a legitimate demand that God prove himself on hostile terms.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise recognize the irony that his words about Peter have just been fulfilled. Mockery cannot discredit the Lord’s truthful knowledge or justify the violence.

verses.text: They spoke many other things against him, insulting him.
verses.arminianNotes: Further insults compound the abuse. Arminian readers recognize the seriousness of degrading speech and resist treating contempt as harmless when directed at a hated opponent.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see sin expressed in words as well as blows. Christ’s patient endurance does not turn his captors’ insults into morally acceptable conduct.

verses.text: As soon as it was day, the assembly of the elders of the people were gathered together, both chief priests and scribes, and they led him away into their council, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The elders, chief priests, and scribes gather at daybreak for council. Arminian readers distinguish institutional authority from a righteous verdict without extending blame to an entire people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise recognize that official procedure can serve hostility rather than truth. The named leadership’s actions do not justify collective condemnation of Jewish people across time.

verses.text: “If you are the Christ, tell us.” But he said to them, “If I tell you, you won’t believe,
verses.arminianNotes: The council’s question meets Jesus’ diagnosis of unbelief. Arminian readers emphasize culpable resistance to testimony rather than assume that further words necessarily produce willing trust.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see unbelief’s moral resistance. The exchange illustrates the need for renewing grace without making the questioners innocent or reducing faith to possession of information.

verses.text: and if I ask, you will in no way answer me or let me go.
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus exposes unwillingness to answer fairly or release him. Arminian readers see refusal of honest engagement as responsible resistance, not a neutral search awaiting one more fact.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise recognize hostility shaping the hearing. Sin affects the will as well as understanding, so a formally religious question need not express openness to truth.

verses.text: From now on, the Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of the power of God.”
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus answers humiliation with the promise of exaltation at God’s right hand. Arminian readers place hope in the vindicated Son rather than the council’s assessment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise confess the authority of the exalted Christ. The courtroom reversal rests on who he is and God’s purpose, not on his receiving human approval.

verses.text: They all said, “Are you then the Son of God?” He said to them, “You say it, because I am.”
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus’ answer acknowledges the identity they put to him. Arminian readers attend to his claim in the flow of the hearing rather than weakening it into mere evasion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise connect the Son of God question with the preceding promise of exaltation. Christ’s identity remains central even while his hearers use his words against him.

verses.text: They said, “Why do we need any more witness? For we ourselves have heard from his own mouth!”
verses.arminianNotes: The council treats Jesus’ own words as sufficient against him. Arminian readers see testimony rejected rather than faithfully received, warning that hearing alone is not saving trust.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise distinguish exposure to Christ’s words from believing reception. The hearing ends in condemnation by his opponents, not in a legitimate refutation of his identity.
